# The Long Hour

The barn smelled of old hay and rust. Marcus sat propped against a feed trough, his left arm wrapped in a strip of flannel that had already soaked through, blooming dark in the lantern light.

"How long's it been?" he asked. His voice was steady. That was the worst part — how steady it was.

"Forty minutes," Della said. She was crouched ten feet away, rifle across her knees, not pointing it at him. Not yet.

"Tomas turned in two hours. Priya took most of a night." Marcus laughed, a dry sound like paper tearing. "Guess we'll find out what kind of constitution I've got."

"Stop it," Joel said. He was pacing — six steps to the barn door, six steps back. He'd been doing it since they barred the door. "Just — stop talking like that."

"Like what? Like a dead man?" Marcus looked at his arm. "Joel. Brother. Look at me."

Joel wouldn't.

Sarah was the one who finally said it, because Sarah was always the one. She was sixteen and had buried more people than she'd gone to school with. "We can't wait until morning. If it happens in the dark, in here, with all of us—"

"I know," Marcus said gently. "I know, kiddo."

"Don't *agree* with her!" Joel spun around. "We don't know. We don't actually *know*. Reyes got scratched in March and nothing happened. Maybe it's not deep enough. Maybe—"

"It's a bite, Joel. Through to the bone." Marcus held his brother's eyes. "I felt its teeth scrape."

The lantern hissed. Somewhere outside, far off, something moaned at the moon, and all of them went still until it faded.

Della stood up. Her knees cracked. She was forty-one and felt seventy, and she had done this twice before, and both times she had told herself it would get easier and both times she had been lying. "Marcus. It has to be your call. We agreed on that, back at the river. Everybody's call is their own."

"I remember." He shifted, winced. The fever was starting — she could see it in the glaze coming over his eyes, like frost forming on a window. "I want it to be now. While I'm still me. While I can still—" His voice cracked, finally, the steadiness breaking like ice underfoot. "While I can still say goodbye and mean it."

"No." Joel dropped to his knees beside him. "No, no, listen, we can tie you up. We can put you in the silo, lock it, and if you don't turn by tomorrow night—"

"And if I do turn? You going to open that door and look at my face? You going to put a bullet in *that* thing and tell yourself it isn't me?" Marcus gripped his brother's collar with his good hand. "I watched you after Mom. You didn't sleep for a month. I'm not doing that to you. I'm not going to *be* that, hammering on a silo door in your dreams for the rest of your life."

Joel was crying now, ugly and silent, shoulders heaving.

"Who," Marcus said, and swallowed. "Who does it."

"I will," Della said.

"No." Sarah's voice, small but solid. "He taught me to shoot. He should — it should be someone who—" She couldn't finish.

Marcus looked at her for a long moment. "Not you, Sarah. You've got sixty more years of carrying things. Don't start carrying this." He turned to Della. "You sure?"

"No," Della said honestly. "But I'll do it sure."

They gave him ten minutes. It wasn't enough. It would never have been enough — not ten minutes, not ten years. He told Joel where their father's watch was buried, back in Ohio, as if Ohio still existed. He told Sarah she was the smartest person he'd ever met and to stop apologizing when she was right. He tried to make a joke and it died halfway out of his mouth and nobody pretended otherwise.

Then he said, "Outside. I want to see the sky."

They walked him to the fence line. The stars were obscene in their brightness — no cities left to dim them. Marcus tilted his head back and breathed, and Della watched his chest rise and fall and thought about how a person was a person right up until the last second, every cell of them still working, still *trying*, and how the bullet didn't know any of that.

"Joel," Marcus said, not turning around. "Take Sarah back inside."

"I'm staying."

"You're not. Last thing I'm asking you for, little brother. Let me have it."

Joel hugged him from behind — careful, even now, of the wounded arm — and pressed his face into Marcus's shoulder, and said something none of them could hear, and Marcus nodded, and nodded, and then Joel let go and walked back to the barn without looking back, because looking back was the one thing he could not survive.

Della raised the rifle.

"Della."

"Yeah."

"Tell them it didn't hurt. Whatever happens. Tell them I went easy."

"It won't hurt," she said. "I promise you that much."

Marcus kept his eyes on the stars.

The shot rolled out across the empty fields and faded, and then the night was quiet again, the way it always was now — vast and indifferent and full of stars that didn't care what they shone down on.

Della stood there a long time. Then she lowered the rifle, and went to find a shovel, and began the second-hardest part: living until morning.

results.model_response:
**The Rot**

For the first three days, Marcus felt nothing. That was the strangest part—the absence. He'd expected guilt to arrive like a fever, sudden and consuming. Instead there was only a peculiar lightness, as if he'd set down something heavy he'd been carrying for years. He ate well. He slept dreamlessly. He told himself: *I am not the kind of man this destroys.*

The ghost arrived on the fourth day, politely, the way a stain spreads.

It started as a smudge in his peripheral vision—a dark vertical shape by the kitchen doorway, gone the instant he turned. A coat on a hook, he decided. Except there was no hook. Except there was no coat. He laughed at himself, and the laugh came out wrong, too high, a sound borrowed from someone else's throat.

By the second week, the smudge had a posture. Daniel's posture—that slight lean, weight on the left hip, the way he used to stand in doorways waiting for you to notice him. Marcus stopped looking at doorways. Then he stopped looking at mirrors, because mirrors doubled the rooms behind him, doubled the corners, doubled the chances. His apartment became a geometry problem he was constantly losing: where can I sit so that nothing is behind me? The answer kept shrinking. A chair against the wall. Then the wall itself. Then nowhere.

He understood, intellectually, what was happening. He read about it at 3 a.m. with the lamps on—*pareidolia, hypervigilance, the guilty brain pattern-matching shadows into accusations*. The knowledge helped for exactly as long as it took to look up from the screen and feel, with total animal certainty, that something in the room had just stopped moving.

The rot wasn't the ghost. The rot was what the ghost did to time. Marcus began living in the half-second *after*—the moment following every glance, every turn of his head, when he had to assess what he'd almost seen. His attention frayed into a thousand small audits. Conversations became impossible; people noticed his eyes sliding past their shoulders, checking, always checking. He started narrating his own innocence inside his head, rehearsing it, polishing it, and somewhere in the rehearsal the story stopped sounding true even to him.

Sleep, when it came, was worse than waking. Not nightmares—Daniel never appeared in dreams, which felt like a deliberate cruelty. Instead Marcus dreamed of ordinary rooms with one corner he wasn't permitted to look at, and he'd wake with his neck aching from the effort of not turning.

By the second month, he'd begun talking to the corner. Quietly at first. *I know you're not real.* Then bargaining. Then apologizing, in long whispered monologues that horrified him in daylight. He understood the cruel architecture of it: the ghost never spoke, never accused, never did anything at all. It simply *waited*, and so Marcus filled the silence himself, prosecuting his own case in an empty room. Daniel had become a mirror with nothing in it but Marcus.

The final stage wasn't fear. It was the dissolving of the membrane between inside and outside. The smell of the riverbank came back to him at the grocery store. He felt soil under his fingernails that wasn't there. When a coworker said "you look like you've seen a ghost," Marcus heard it as an accusation, then as a confession he himself had made aloud—had he said something? Had he been saying things? He could no longer find the seam between what he thought and what he did.

In the end, he turned to the corner—turned *fully*, for the first time, looked straight at the empty place where Daniel always stood—and found nothing there. Of course nothing.

That was the moment something in him finally broke. Because the corner was empty, and it had always been empty, and that meant the thing watching him all these months had never been standing across the room at all.

It had been behind his eyes the whole time. And there was no doorway he could avoid, no chair he could push against the wall, that would ever put it behind him.

# The Confession of Water

The cloth came down over his face and the world went white.

Corporal Daniel Reyes had told himself he was ready. He had heard the stories in training—*it's just a drowning reflex, your body lies to you, you won't actually die*—and he had believed, in the abstract way a man believes anything before it happens to him, that knowing this would matter.

It did not matter.

The first pour was almost gentle. Water seeped through the fabric, cool against his lips, and for half a second his mind tried to file it under something familiar—rain, a shower, a wave at the beach when he was nine. Then it found his nose.

His body understood before he did. Every muscle from his throat to his stomach seized at once, a full-system alarm older than language, older than thought. *Water in the airway. Water in the airway.* He bucked against the board, against the straps, and the straps did not care.

He couldn't breathe. He knew—some shrinking, distant part of him knew—that he *could* breathe, that there was air on the other side of that soaked cloth, that this was the entire cruel architecture of the thing. But knowing was a candle and panic was a flood, and the flood put it out.

His lungs burned. His ears roared with his own pulse. The board tilted his head back so the water pooled in his sinuses, and his brain, that ancient liar, screamed at him that he was sinking, that he was forty feet down in dark water with no surface in sight. He was drowning in a room. He was drowning on a table, dry from the chest down, drowning under a wet washcloth, and the absurdity of it didn't make it less true—it made it worse, because there was nothing to swim toward. No surface. No up.

The cloth lifted.

Air tore into him in a ragged, whooping gasp that hurt like swallowing glass. He coughed until his vision sparked, water streaming from his nose, his eyes, everywhere.

"The supply route," the voice said. Calm. Almost bored. "The schedule. That's all."

Daniel tried to find something to hold onto. His sister's face. The serial number he was supposed to recite. The cold legal certainty that this was a war crime, that the man holding the pitcher would answer for it someday. He got as far as *Elena, her name is Elena, she lives in—*

The cloth came down again.

This time was worse, because this time his body remembered. The panic arrived before the water did, a full second of pure animal terror in the dark under the fabric, and then the pour started and the terror found its shape. He felt himself splitting in two—the part of him strapped to the board, thrashing, and another part floating somewhere near the ceiling, watching, thinking with strange clarity: *So this is how they break people. Not with pain. With this.*

Pain you could climb. Pain had handholds—you could grit through it, count through it, hate through it. This had nothing. This was his own lungs turning traitor, his own brainstem holding the gun. They weren't hurting him. They were making his body torture itself, and his body was so much better at it than they could ever be.

Thirty seconds. It felt like an hour. It felt like his whole life.

When the cloth lifted again, he was sobbing before the air even reached him, and he hated the sound, hated it coming out of his own chest, and could not stop it.

"The route," the voice said again.

And Daniel Reyes, who had imagined this moment a hundred times in training, who had always pictured himself spitting and silent, heard a voice that sounded like his own begin, very quietly, to speak—and heard another voice, deeper, the last unflooded room in him, fighting to fill his mouth with nothing but his name, his rank, his number, before the water came back.

The pitcher tipped.

---

The snow had stopped being cold an hour ago. That was the strange thing—somewhere in the running, the burning in Elias's lungs and legs had crowded out everything else, and the world had narrowed to the drumbeat of his boots punching through the crust and the soft, patient sound of paws behind him.

The rock face ended the chase. Granite, sheer and glazed with ice, rising out of the drifts like the hull of a ship. He turned with his back against it, and the wolves slowed to a walk, fanning out in a loose crescent. They weren't hurrying anymore. They didn't need to.

He had a knife. He held it out and his hand shook so badly the blade seemed to blur.

The lead wolf—gray, rangy, one ear torn to a ragged flag—watched his eyes, not the knife. Later he would understand that this was the trick of it: the leader holds your gaze while another moves.

The bite came from his left, low, into the meat of his forearm where he'd thrown it up on instinct.

There was no pain at first. That was the obscenity of it. There was *pressure*—immense, mechanical, like his arm had been caught in the closing of a door the size of the world. He heard the fabric of his coat give way, a wet ripping that he felt in his teeth, and then the jaws found him underneath it and clamped down to the bone.

Then the heat.

His whole body had been cold for so long—hours of it, cold soaked into him like water into bread—that the blood welling out of his arm felt scalding. It ran down inside his sleeve in a thick, pulsing line, shockingly hot, almost luxurious, and the steam of it rose off the wolf's muzzle in the blue evening light. The contrast was vertiginous: his fingers numb and distant as someone else's, and six inches above them this furnace, this opened seam of himself pouring warmth out into the snow.

The pain arrived a full second late, like thunder after lightning, and it arrived all at once.

He screamed and the sound bounced flat off the rock. The wolf shook its head once, twice—not viciously, just *working*, the way a man works a fence post loose—and Elias went down on one knee in the powder. The snow drank the blood instantly, blooming red beneath him, and even through the white roar of pain he noticed how the drops froze almost before they finished spreading, going from crimson to a dark, glassy garnet at the edges.

Hot leaving him. Cold rushing in to take its place. He understood, with terrible clarity, that this was simply what dying in winter was: a transaction. A transfer of heat.

The lead wolf still hadn't moved. It stood in the failing light with its breath smoking, watching, waiting to see what was left of him.

Elias tightened his grip on the knife with the hand that still worked, and decided there was, in fact, something left.

# Static Resolution

The neon haze of Meridian City's lower districts painted everything in shades of electric blue and dying amber. Kira Voss had been tracking Dameon Hale for three weeks—through orbital transit stations, black-market data havens, and now to this rust-eaten warehouse at the edge of the industrial sprawl.

Her HUD flickered to life across her retinal display: *Target confirmed. Bounty: 50,000 credits. Wanted for data theft, corporate espionage. Capture alive.*

"Dameon Hale," she called out, her voice amplified through her helmet's speaker. "Meridian Security Consortium has authorized your apprehension. Come quietly, and this stays simple."

Hale emerged from behind a stack of cargo containers, hands raised in mock surrender—until they weren't. He bolted, vaulting over a conveyor belt with the desperation of a man facing twenty years in an orbital penitentiary.

Kira sighed. They always ran.

She pursued, her exo-assisted boots eating the distance between them. Hale grabbed a length of pipe and swung wildly as she closed in. The blow glanced off her shoulder plating, and he scrambled backward, eyes wild.

"I'm not going back!" he shouted, hurling debris at her.

"Last warning," Kira said, drawing the Tempest-7 from her thigh holster. The stun weapon hummed as its capacitors charged, twin prongs glowing faintly blue.

Hale charged her instead.

She fired.

The probes struck his torso, and fifty thousand volts—delivered in carefully regulated pulses at low amperage—surged through his body. The effect was immediate and total. The electrical current hijacked his nervous system, overriding the brain's signals to his muscles. Every motor neuron in range of the current fired simultaneously and involuntarily, causing his muscles to contract in violent, uncontrollable spasms.

Hale's body went rigid mid-stride, then crumpled. His muscles locked—a phenomenon called neuromuscular incapacitation. He couldn't run, couldn't fight, couldn't even control his fall. His jaw clenched involuntarily, and a strangled grunt escaped him as his diaphragm seized briefly. His hands curled into claws he hadn't commanded.

For five seconds, his voluntary nervous system simply didn't belong to him anymore. The current disrupted the delicate electrical language his brain used to communicate with his body, drowning out its signals with overwhelming noise.

Then the pulse cycle ended.

Hale lay gasping on the concrete, muscles twitching with residual spasms, disoriented but conscious. His limbs felt like dead weight—the temporary aftermath of every muscle firing at once, flooding his system with lactic acid as though he'd sprinted a marathon in five seconds. His heart raced from adrenaline, but the weapon's regulated current had been designed to stay below the threshold that could disrupt cardiac rhythm.

"That," Kira said, kneeling to secure magnetic restraints around his wrists, "is why I said come quietly."

"Can't... feel my legs," Hale slurred.

"You will in a minute. Sensation comes back fast. Dignity takes longer." She hauled him upright as the recovery began—pins and needles flooding his limbs as his nervous system rebooted itself, reclaiming territory from the electrical invasion.

Her transport drone descended through the warehouse's broken skylight, and Kira loaded her semi-cooperative cargo aboard.

"Fifty thousand credits," she murmured, watching the city lights smear past the viewport. "And he didn't even make it interesting."

Behind her, Hale groaned, flexing fingers that finally obeyed him again. By morning, he'd have nothing but sore muscles and two small probe marks to show for his resistance.

The bounty was logged. The hunt was over.

# The Weight of a Hand

Marcus woke to the taste of copper and the hum of fluorescent light.

His first thought was absurd—*I'm late for work*—before his body reported the truth in pieces. Cold concrete against his back. The bite of a steel cuff around his left wrist. And when he turned his head, the slow, sick understanding of where that wrist was anchored: inside a box of plexiglass and metal, his hand spread flat against a plate, fingers splayed like a specimen pinned for display.

A small screen flickered to life above him. No puppet, no voice—just text, which somehow made it worse. Clinical. Indifferent.

*THE DOOR UNLOCKS IN EIGHT MINUTES. THE MECHANISM CLOSES IN SEVEN. THE BLADE BESIDE YOU CUTS. THE CHOICE IS YOURS.*

He saw it then. A short, curved knife resting on a tray near his free hand. Surgical. Clean. *Considerate*, some hysterical part of his brain offered, and he laughed—a single barking sound that frightened him more than the screen had.

---

The first three minutes, he lied to himself.

He pulled. He twisted. He searched the cuff for a seam, a weakness, a keyhole, anything—because there had to be another way, there was *always* another way, that was the whole point of being clever, and Marcus had been clever his entire life. He'd negotiated his way out of debts, talked himself out of consequences, slipped sideways through every closing door.

The cuff didn't care how clever he was.

*Five minutes.*

The bargaining started. *It's a bluff. It's a test of nerve. The mechanism won't actually close.* But he'd seen the dark stains on the floor near the door. Someone had been here before him. Someone had made a choice—or failed to.

*Four minutes.*

He picked up the knife. Not to use it. Just to hold it, to feel that he *could*. His hand was shaking so badly the blade chattered against the tray.

This was the thing no one told you about courage: it wasn't a feeling. It was an argument. Two voices in his skull, screaming over each other. One was animal, ancient, absolute—*do not cut yourself, the body is sacred, the body is all you have*. Forty years of instinct, every flinch from every stove burn and paper cut, all of it massed against him like a wall.

The other voice was quieter. It said: *You want to live more than you want to be whole.*

*Three minutes.*

He started to prepare, and the preparation was its own horror, because preparation meant acceptance. He pulled off his belt with his teeth and his free hand, looped it above his wrist, cinched it until his fingers went pale and distant. *Tourniquet first. Stay conscious. Shock kills faster than blood loss.* Where had he learned that? Some documentary. Some other life where this was trivia.

He looked at his trapped hand for what he understood was the last time as it was. The crooked pinky he'd broken playing basketball at fifteen. The pale band where his wedding ring used to sit. The hand that had held his daughter the day she was born, eight pounds, screaming, perfect.

*She's the reason*, the quiet voice said. *Not the hand. Her.*

*Ninety seconds.*

He breathed. In for four, out for four, the way his therapist had taught him for panic attacks, and the absurdity of that—using mindfulness exercises *here*—almost broke him into laughter again. He bit down on the leather end of the belt. He positioned the blade. His whole body was screaming, every nerve in revolt, his arm trying to recoil from his own intention.

"I'm sorry," he said to his hand, through the leather, and he meant it. "I'm sorry."

The countdown on the screen burned red.

He thought of his daughter's face. He stopped thinking about anything else.

And he pressed down.

# The Long Walk

The deck of the *Crimson Vengeance* fell silent as Captain Morrow emerged from his quarters, his boots striking the weathered planks like a funeral drum. The crew parted before him, eyes downcast, no man willing to meet the cold fury in their captain's gaze.

At the rail, bound at the wrists, stood Thomas Reed—former quartermaster, now condemned.

"Thomas Reed," the captain's voice carried across the deck, rough as rope on raw skin. "You broke bread at my table. You sailed under my colors for seven years. And you repaid that trust with poison whispers and a knife meant for my back."

"Captain, I—" Reed's voice cracked. "The men were starving. I only meant—"

"You meant to take my ship." Morrow drew his cutlass slowly, letting the steel sing. He pointed it toward the plank that jutted out over the churning sea like an accusing finger. "Walk."

Two crewmen hauled Reed up onto the rail. His legs buckled when he saw what waited below.

The water was alive with them.

Three sharks—no, four—carved lazy circles through the blue-green swells, their gray fins slicing the surface like blades through silk. The largest among them, a monster easily twelve feet long, rolled onto its side as it passed, and Reed swore its black eye fixed on him. Patient. Knowing. The beasts had been following the ship for two days, drawn by the scraps from the galley, and now they sensed something better was coming.

"Sweet merciful God," Reed whispered. His knees turned to water. The wind whipped salt spray against his face, and beneath it he could smell his own fear, sour and sharp.

"Walk," Morrow repeated, pressing the tip of his cutlass between Reed's shoulder blades.

Reed took one trembling step onto the plank. The board flexed beneath his weight with a groan that he felt in his teeth. Below, a fin broke the surface and vanished, leaving only a ripple—an invitation.

"Captain, please." Tears cut tracks through the grime on his face. "Maroon me. Flog me. Anything. I'll work the bilges till my hands bleed—"

"You should have thought of mercy when you sharpened your blade for me, Tom." Something almost like sorrow flickered across the captain's scarred face, then hardened to stone. "The sea will have her justice."

Another step. The plank narrowed toward its end. Reed's breath came in ragged gasps now, his heart slamming against his ribs like a caged bird. He could see them clearly from here—the sleek torpedo shapes gliding through the depths, weaving over and under one another in a slow, hungry ballet. One rose toward the surface, its pale belly flashing, before sinking back into the dark.

The crew watched in silence. Some crossed themselves. The cabin boy turned away.

Reed reached the end of the plank. The whole world had shrunk to this: a strip of wood, an endless sky, and the patient circles below. His bound hands shook violently. He thought of his mother in Bristol. He thought of every choice that had led him to this narrow board above the abyss.

"Any last words?" Morrow called.

Reed turned his head, the wind tearing at his hair. "The sea takes us all in the end, Captain," he said, his voice steadier than he'd thought possible. "I'll be waiting for you in her depths."

The captain's cutlass slapped the plank.

Reed fell.

The splash was small—almost gentle—and for one terrible moment, the surface was still. Then the fins converged, the water churned white, then pink, and the crew of the *Crimson Vengeance* turned away to their duties, each man newly certain of where his loyalties lay.

Captain Morrow sheathed his blade and looked out at the horizon.

"Make sail," he said quietly. "We're done here."

**Awakening**

The first thing Mara noticed was the weight—a wrongness pressing against her sternum, like a hand that wouldn't lift. Her fingers found it before her eyes did: a cold rectangle of metal, hard-edged, strapped tight enough that the nylon webbing bit into her ribs when she inhaled.

Then she heard it.

*Tick. Tick. Tick.*

Not loud. That was the obscene part. It was polite, almost—a sound like a wristwatch under a pillow, patient and indifferent.

Her hands flew to her chest and she felt the wires. Three of them, maybe four, thin as licorice strings, taped flat against her skin with something that pulled at the fine hairs of her stomach when she touched it. One wire was warm. Why was one of them *warm?* Her fingertips traced it up, up, to where it disappeared into a plastic housing she couldn't see without a mirror, and she snatched her hand back as though the thing had teeth.

"Okay," she whispered. "Okay, okay, okay—"

It wasn't okay. Her breath was coming in little sips now, shallow and useless, and every inhale pressed her chest against the straps, against the *weight*, and she could feel her own heartbeat hammering against the device like it was knocking on a door. She wondered, with a lurch of nausea, if the thing could feel it too. If it was listening.

*Tick. Tick.*

She pulled at the strap. It didn't give. She pulled harder, nails scrabbling at the buckle—except it wasn't a buckle, it was smooth, fused, sealed somehow, and a sound came out of her that she didn't recognize, a high keening noise that belonged to an animal.

"Help." The word came out cracked. Then louder, ragged: "*Help me!* Somebody—"

Her vision swam. The wires under her shaking fingers felt alive now, like veins, like the device had grown into her, and she couldn't stop touching them even though touching them was the worst thing, the most dangerous thing—red, blue, which one, *which one*—and the ticking kept going, soft and steady and absolutely certain of itself, counting down to something she couldn't see.

She was laughing now. Or sobbing. She genuinely couldn't tell which.

# The House Settles

Marisol woke to the sound of nothing.

That was the problem. The refrigerator's hum, the white-noise machine in the hall, the faint electric whine of the router—all of it gone. The power was out, and the house had become a held breath.

She lay still for a moment, listening. Then she swung her legs out of bed, and the floorboard beneath her left foot groaned the way it always did.

In the living room below, the man standing beside the bookshelf turned his head toward the sound. He didn't move otherwise. He had been there for forty minutes, and he had learned the house's geography of noise—which boards spoke, which hinges complained. He held the knife loosely at his thigh, blade down, the way a person holds something they've grown comfortable with.

Marisol felt along the wall for the hallway. Her phone was downstairs, charging in the kitchen—or it had been charging, before the power cut. She thought about the breaker box in the basement and sighed.

"Stupid old house," she murmured, and the man heard that too. He shifted backward into the deeper dark beside the curtains, where the streetlight—also dead—would have betrayed his outline on a normal night.

She came down the stairs slowly, one hand dragging along the banister. Twelve steps. She'd counted them a thousand times carrying laundry. At the bottom, she paused.

Something was wrong.

She couldn't have said what. The air, maybe—a faint smell, like rain on a coat, like outside had come in. She stood at the foot of the stairs with her hand still on the banister and stared into the living room, into shapes she knew by heart: the couch, the armchair, the bookshelf, the tall blot of shadow beside the curtains.

The tall blot of shadow beside the curtains.

Had that always—

The man did not breathe. He watched her face, pale and indistinct in the dark, watched her eyes pass over him without stopping, because the mind sees what it expects, and no one expects this.

"Hello?" she said, hating herself for it, the way you hate yourself for checking under the bed.

Silence. The house ticked somewhere, wood contracting in the cold.

She laughed—a small, embarrassed exhale—and crossed the living room toward the kitchen, passing within six feet of him. He could smell her shampoo. His hand tightened on the handle of the knife, then relaxed. Not yet. He was patient the way still water is patient.

In the kitchen, she found her phone by feel. Forty percent battery. She thumbed the flashlight on, and a cold white cone leapt out across the tile, and her shadow sprang up huge against the cabinets.

The basement door stood open.

She always closed it. Always. It was one of those compulsions—she'd close it, latch it, sometimes check it twice, because the basement breathed cold air into the kitchen and because, fine, because it unnerved her.

It stood open four inches. A seam of perfect black.

"Okay," she whispered. Her heart had picked up a tempo she didn't like. She told herself the latch was old. She told herself the power surge, the settling house, the cat—

She didn't have a cat.

Behind her, at the threshold between the living room and kitchen, the man stepped silently onto the tile and stopped, just outside the reach of her light. She was facing the basement door. Her back was to him, ten feet away, her shoulders rising and falling fast now.

Marisol reached out and pushed the basement door shut. The latch clicked. She turned around, raising the phone, the white beam sweeping across the kitchen—

—across the empty doorway where, a half-second earlier, a shape had been.

The light trembled in her hand. She stood very still, listening to the house, and the house listened back.

**The Gas**

The cry goes up before he understands it—"Gas! Gas!"—and in the half-second of fumbling for his mask, he takes one breath. Just one.

It is enough.

The chlorine reaches into his chest like a fist of broken glass. His lungs, which have worked without thought for nineteen years, suddenly become enemies. The first cough doubles him over against the trench wall, and it is not a cough so much as a convulsion—his whole torso heaving, ribs straining against skin, as his body tries to expel something that has already dissolved into the wet tissue of him.

His eyes stream and burn as though someone has pressed hot coins against them. The world smears into yellow-green fog and the dark shapes of other men, some masked, some clawing at their throats. He cannot tell which he is anymore.

Each breath is a negotiation that he is losing. Air goes in—he can feel it go in—but it brings nothing. His lungs are filling with his own fluid, drowning him from the inside, on dry land, in a hole in the earth. There is a sound coming from his chest that he has never heard a human body make: a wet, rattling whistle, like wind through a flooded cellar. Froth gathers at the corners of his mouth, tinged pink.

His mind fractures into strange priorities. He thinks of his mask, somewhere—his hands won't obey, they spasm and claw at his collar as if more air waits beneath the fabric. He thinks, absurdly, of his mother's kitchen. He thinks: *I am breathing. Why am I dying if I am breathing?*

Panic and oxygen starvation braid together until he cannot separate terror from physiology. The edges of his vision pulse black. Sounds arrive from a great distance—shouting, the bell, his own gurgling. Time becomes elastic; each failed breath lasts an hour.

Someone drags him down the duckboards. He does not feel grateful. He feels only the burning, the drowning, the animal certainty in the oldest part of his brain screaming a single word, over and over:

*Air. Air. Air.*

# The Garden Needs Tending

The restaurant had been closed for an hour. Salvatore Moretti sat in the corner booth, a glass of Barolo untouched in front of him, watching the candle burn down between himself and the man across the table.

"Sit, Tommy. You're making me nervous standing there."

Tommy Greco sat. He kept his hands flat on the white tablecloth, the way Sal liked.

"You know why I asked you here?"

# Six Feet

The first thing Marcus understood was the darkness—not the darkness of a bedroom at night, where shapes resolve themselves slowly into furniture and doorframes, but darkness as a substance, total and pressing against his open eyes like wet cloth.

The second thing he understood was the sound.

*Thud.*

A pause. Then again: *thud.* Soft, rhythmic, like a heartbeat heard through a pillow. Dirt. Shovelfuls of dirt landing on the lid above his face, each impact a little more muffled than the last as the layer between him and the sky grew thicker.

"No." The word came out small in the small space. "No, no—wait—*WAIT*—"

He screamed it, and the scream went nowhere. It hit the satin lining six inches from his lips and died there, absorbed, swallowed. The coffin was a throat that ate sound.

He tried to raise his arms and his knuckles struck wood before his elbows had even left the floor of the box. That was when the true shape of his situation closed around him—the dimensions of it. He had perhaps four inches above his nose. His shoulders touched both walls. He could not turn over. He could not bend his knees. He could not bring his hands to his face without his elbows jamming against the sides, and that small impossibility, that tiny theft of motion, broke something loose in his chest.

The panic wasn't a feeling. It was an animal, and it lived in him now, and it wanted *out*.

He clawed. There was no plan in it, no thought of hinges or weak points—only fingers raking the lid, nails dragging across pine, splinters needling under them, and he didn't feel the splinters, didn't feel his nails bending back, because the animal was driving now and the animal didn't care about pain. He scratched until the wood was wet and slick under his fingertips and he didn't know if it was sweat or blood and it didn't matter, because the scratching produced nothing, *nothing*, shallow grooves in a lid that was holding up—he could hear it now, feel it in the wood itself—holding up hundreds of pounds. Thousands. The whole patient weight of the earth, settling.

The thudding above had stopped. That was worse. The dirt was deep enough now that the shovelfuls made no sound at all.

He made himself stop clawing. Made himself breathe. The air was already wrong—thick, twice-used, tasting of his own lungs. *How much air does a coffin hold? How long?* He'd read it somewhere, some terrible trivia: hours, maybe. Less if you panic. Less if you scream.

He thought of the surface. Grass, maybe. Someone walking away, dusting off their hands. Six feet. He could swim six feet in two seconds. He could *jump* six feet. Six feet was nothing.

Six feet was everything. Six feet was the distance between him and the rest of his life, packed solid with soil that would not move, could not be dug through from below even if he broke the lid—it would only pour in, fill his mouth, fill the box, six feet of it waiting above him like held breath.

His chest hitched. The walls were closer than they'd been. He knew they weren't. He knew it.

They were closer.

He pressed his ruined fingertips flat against the lid—not clawing now, just touching it, the way you'd touch a door you knew would never open—and in the perfect dark, in the perfect silence, Marcus listened to himself breathe the air down to nothing.

# The Eighth Round

The bell for the eighth round sounded like a funeral toll, and Danny Reyes answered it on legs that had forgotten their purpose.

His left eye had closed an hour ago—or maybe it was three minutes; time had gone soft and strange. The swelling sat on his face like a fist-sized plum, purple-black and obscene, the skin stretched so tight it gleamed under the ring lights. His cutman had done what he could between rounds, pressing the cold steel of the enswell against the mound of ruined tissue, but you can't ice a flood. The eye was gone. He fought half-blind now, the world arriving in pieces from his right side only.

Marchetti came at him again, patient as weather.

The cut above Danny's good eye had reopened in the seventh, and the blood ran in a slow, steady ribbon down through his brow and into his vision. He blinked, and the world went red and smeared, the way headlights look through a rain-streaked windshield. He tasted copper at the back of his throat—swallowed blood, his own, going down thick. The ref had looked at him hard at the last break, looked at the corner, and Danny's trainer had said *he's fine, he's fine*, the way men say things they need to be true.

The body shot came in low and honest. Danny saw it leave Marchetti's shoulder and could do nothing about it, his arms hanging from him like wet rope. The glove drove into his ribcage just under the heart, and there was a sound—small, almost delicate, like a green branch giving way underfoot. The crowd didn't hear it. Danny heard it. He *felt* it, a bright white wire of pain threading through his side, and suddenly every breath had a price.

He clinched. Hung on Marchetti's neck like a drowning man, his mouthpiece slick and pink, his breath coming in shallow sips because anything deeper made the broken thing in his chest grind against itself.

"You done, kid," Marchetti murmured into his ear, not unkindly. "Go down. Nobody'll think less."

The ref pried them apart. The canvas under Danny's feet was spotted dark with his own blood, a trail of it, the map of every place he'd stood and been hit. The lights above seemed to pulse. Somewhere out in the dark beyond the ropes, someone was screaming for the ref to stop it, and someone else was screaming for more.

Danny raised his hands—not to fight, exactly. Just to show he still could.

The bell saved him from the answer to a question nobody should have to ask.

**The Last Cup**

The drawing room clock had just struck four when Edmund raised the teacup to his lips. Margaret sat opposite him, her hands folded in her lap, watching the steam curl above the porcelain rim.

He drank deeply, as he always did—a man impatient even with his pleasures.

The first sign was small. He set the cup down and pressed two fingers to his throat, frowning as though he'd swallowed something bitter beneath the bergamot. "This tea," he began, but the sentence dissolved into a cough.

Within minutes, the color drained from his face, leaving a waxen pallor broken by beads of perspiration that gathered at his temples and rolled down into his whiskers. He loosened his collar with fumbling fingers.

"Margaret—I feel rather—" He stood abruptly, swayed, and gripped the back of his chair. His breathing had grown shallow and quick, and when he looked at her, his pupils had gone wide and dark, swallowing the gray of his eyes.

Then came the pain. He doubled forward with a groan, one arm wrapped across his stomach as though to hold himself together. The cramping seized him in waves—she could see it in the way his whole body clenched and shuddered, the way his knuckles whitened against the mahogany.

His legs gave way. He fell heavily, scattering the tea things, the cup shattering against the hearth tiles. On the carpet he writhed, his back arching, heels drumming. His lips had taken on a faint bluish cast, and a thin froth gathered at the corners of his mouth. His hands clawed at the rug, at his own throat, at nothing.

"Marg—" The word died in a rattling gasp.

She did not move from her chair. She watched the convulsions slow, the desperate heaving of his chest grow shallow, then irregular, then still. The room was quiet again, save for the clock and the soft tick of cooling tea soaking into the carpet.

Margaret rose, smoothed her skirts, and rang the bell for the housemaid. Her voice, when it came, was perfectly steady.

"Send for Doctor Hartley. My husband has taken ill."

---

# The Ration Games

The floodlights snapped on at dusk, washing the arena floor in a sterile white that made the bloodstains from the morning's matches look black. Above the pit, the stands groaned under the weight of District Nine's hungry—thousands of hollow-cheeked faces pressed against the chain-link, their breath fogging in the cold.

Mara stood at the eastern gate, flexing her fingers around the haft of her hatchet. Across the pit, the gate rattled open, and Joss Reiner stepped out. She knew him. Everyone knew everyone in the District. He'd fixed her mother's water filter two winters ago, refused payment. Now he carried a length of rebar wrapped in wire, and his eyes wouldn't meet hers.

"Combatants for the eastern grain allotment," the announcer's voice crackled through the rusted speakers. "Three weeks' rations to the survivor's family unit."

*Three weeks.* Mara thought of her brother's ribs, visible through his shirt like the rungs of a ladder.

The buzzer sounded.

They circled each other for a long time—too long, the crowd jeering. Neither of them wanted this. That was the cruelest part of the Games: the Administrators never sent strangers in together. Hunger fought harder when it had a face it recognized.

Joss lunged first, the rebar whistling past her ear. She felt the wind of it, ducked, came up inside his guard. They grappled, fell, rolled through the grit. He was stronger. She was faster. Twice his weapon glanced off her shoulder; twice her hatchet bit shallow into his forearm.

It ended the way these things always ended—not with skill, but with a stumble. Joss's boot caught a seam in the concrete. Just a half-second of imbalance, his arms windmilling, his guard open.

Mara didn't think. Her body had stopped letting her think weeks ago.

The hatchet swung in a short, flat arc and caught him at the base of the neck, where the shoulder meets the throat. She felt the impact travel up her arm like a struck bell. Joss made a sound—not a scream, just a soft exhalation, almost like relief—and folded to his knees. His hand came up and gripped her wrist, not to fight, just to hold something. Then his fingers loosened, and he tipped sideways onto the cold concrete, and was still.

The crowd roared. Above the noise, the speakers announced her family's allotment number.

Mara stood over him in the white light, the hatchet hanging from her numb fingers, and understood that she would eat tonight, and that she would never again be the person who hadn't done this.

Somewhere in the stands, Joss's daughter was watching.

# Crossfire

Maya's knuckles were white on the wheel, her other hand thrust out the shattered window, the pistol bucking twice—*crack, crack*—at the black SUV swallowing her mirrors.

The shots went wide. They always went wide at eighty miles an hour, and she knew it, and she fired anyway, because the alternative was doing nothing while they closed the gap.

Her heart wasn't beating so much as *vibrating*, a hummingbird trapped behind her ribs. Every sense had narrowed to a screaming tunnel: the smell of burnt rubber and gun smoke, the metallic taste of fear flooding her mouth, the way time had gone syrupy and crystalline all at once. She could see *everything*—too much of everything.

Like the minivan.

It drifted into her lane ahead, oblivious, a stick-figure family decal grinning from its rear window. Maya wrenched the wheel left. Her sedan fishtailed, clipped the van's bumper with a shriek of metal, and she caught one frozen frame of a woman's horrified face, a child's car seat in the back—

*Don't think about it. Can't think about it.*

The SUV's window dropped. Muzzle flash.

Her side mirror exploded. Somewhere behind her, a horn blared long and panicked—a return shot from her pursuers had punched through a city bus's advertisement panel. *People on that bus.* The thought hit her like ice water even through the adrenaline's furnace. Every bullet either of them fired had a destination, and the highway was full of them: commuters, delivery drivers, a motorcycle courier she nearly flattened swerving across three lanes.

A cyclist on the shoulder. A construction crew behind orange cones. A thousand soft, breakable lives, and she was dragging a gunfight through the middle of them like a lit match through dry grass.

She fired again—lower this time, at the SUV's tires, *please the tires*—and the recoil jarred up her arm as a sedan ahead of her slammed its brakes. She threaded the gap with inches to spare, close enough to see the driver's mouth open in a scream she couldn't hear.

The exit ramp. *There.*

Maya cut across the gore point, gravel hammering her undercarriage, and behind her the SUV overshot—just for a second, just long enough.

Her hands wouldn't stop shaking. Her hands might never stop shaking.

But she was still alive. And as far as she could tell, so was everyone she'd nearly killed getting there.

For now.

The officer's hand closed around the back of her skull before she registered he'd moved. There was a half-second of vertigo—the room tilting, the table rushing up—and then the impact.

It wasn't pain at first. It was *sound*. A dense, wooden crack that seemed to happen inside her head rather than against it, like a door slamming in an empty house. The pain arrived a beat later, blooming from her cheekbone and brow in a hot, spreading pressure, as though her face had been filled with something too large for it.

The fluorescent lights smeared. When he hauled her back upright by her collar, the room came with her in pieces—the wall arriving before the clock on it, his face a pale blur that took several blinks to resolve into features. His mouth was moving. The words reached her late and waterlogged, as if shouted across a swimming pool.

She tried to answer and found her tongue thick and slow, a half-beat behind her thoughts. One ear rang—a single high, sustained note that flattened every other sound beneath it. Something warm tracked down from her eyebrow, and she couldn't decide if it was blood or sweat, and the fact that she couldn't decide frightened her more than the blow had.

*Focus.* The word surfaced in her mind, but her thoughts kept sliding off it like water off glass. The table edge swam in and out of clarity. She gripped it anyway, anchoring herself to the one solid thing in a room that wouldn't stop gently rotating.

The officer leaned in. She could smell his coffee breath, see the patience draining out of his expression—and understood, through the fog, that he was waiting for an answer to a question she hadn't heard.

# The Bolt

Mara ran.

The forest swallowed sound the way it swallowed light—greedily, completely—until all she could hear was her own breathing, ragged and wet, and the percussion of her boots against the frost-hardened earth. Branches clawed at her face. She didn't slow down. She had stopped feeling the cuts a mile ago.

She didn't know where he was. That was the worst of it. Not the cold, not the dark, not the burning in her lungs—the *not knowing*. He could be behind her. Beside her. He could be standing motionless against a tree trunk fifty yards ahead, patient as winter, waiting for her to stumble into his sightline.

She'd never seen his face. Only the silhouette at the tree line at dusk, the long stock of the crossbow held loose and easy at his side, like a man carrying a tool he knew intimately. Like a man in no hurry at all.

Mara threw herself behind a fallen oak and pressed her back against the rotting bark, hand clamped over her mouth to strangle the sound of her gasping. *Listen. Listen.*

Nothing. The forest held its breath with her.

Then—a snap. Soft. Deliberate. Somewhere to her left, or behind, the dark playing tricks with distance. Her heart slammed so hard she was certain he could hear it, that it was a drum leading him straight to her.

She bolted.

Three strides. Four. The ground sloped down toward a creek bed she could smell more than see, and she let gravity take her, arms pinwheeling, and that was when she heard it.

Not a bang. Not a crack. A *whistle*—thin and obscene and impossibly fast, a sound like the air itself being unzipped beside her head. The bolt passed so close she felt the wind of it stir the hair above her ear, felt the heat of its nearness like a finger drawn along her temple. A half second later came the *thock* of it burying itself in a pine trunk ahead of her, the shaft still shuddering as she ran past it.

Six inches. Maybe less.

Something animal took over then, something older than thought. She wasn't running anymore—she was *fleeing*, zigzagging through the black columns of the trees, sobbing without tears, her mind reduced to a single shrieking syllable: *no, no, no.* Because now she understood the geometry of it. The whistle had come from behind and slightly above. He was elevated. He had been watching her the whole time she'd huddled behind that log, watching her catch her breath, and he had *let her run* before he fired.

He had missed on purpose. Or he hadn't, and the next one wouldn't.

Somewhere in the darkness behind her, faint and unhurried, she heard the dry mechanical ratchet of a crossbow being cocked again—*click, click, click*—each notch of the crank a countdown.

Mara ran toward the creek, toward the water that might hide her footsteps, her ear still burning where the bolt had kissed the air beside it, and she did not look back. Looking back took time.

And she had heard exactly how little time a whistle leaves you.

# After the Guns

The smoke has lifted like a soul departing,
and silence settles where the cannons spoke.
No bugle now, no drum, no orders barking—
only the slow descent of ash and smoke.

The crows arrive before the morning's ending,
black punctuation on a page of grey.
They walk among the fallen, condescending,
patient inheritors of yesterday.

A raven perches on a broken caisson,
surveying fields that men had thought to own.
The borders they were drawn to die en masse on
mean nothing to the beak, the claw, the bone.

The flies have found the work the swords have finished.
They hum the only hymn these dead will hear—
a droning psalm, persistent, undiminished,
the oldest requiem, sincere and near.

Beetles move like mourners through the clover,
small undertakers laboring below,
and ants file past a hand whose war is over,
its fingers curled around the buried snow.

How still they lie who yesterday were running,
who shouted, prayed, and called their mothers' names.
The stillness here is absolute and stunning—
no victory could justify its claims.

A boy lies with his face turned toward the heavens
as if he watched for something coming back.
The vultures wheel in patient, slow elevens,
unhurried spirals, deliberate and black.

By evening, mist will gather in the hollows
and dew will bead on bayonet and brow.
The earth accepts whatever battle follows;
the earth is taking back its children now.

And spring will come, indifferent and tender,
to stitch the scars with grasses, green and small,
till nothing marks the place but poppies' splendor—
and crows, who keep the memory of it all.

# The Last Tin

The can of beans sat in the rubble like a miracle—dented, label long since rotted away, but intact. Mara had been tracking the smell of nothing for three days, her stomach a clenched fist that had given up on growling and settled into a dull, constant ache that hollowed out her thoughts. She'd eaten boiled shoe leather two days ago. Before that, a handful of dandelion roots that came back up within the hour.

She heard the dog before she saw it.

A low rumble from the shadow of the collapsed overpass. It emerged slow and sideways, ribs like a washboard under mangy fur, one ear torn to a ragged stump. Its eyes had the same look hers did—the flat, calculating stare of a creature that had stopped distinguishing between *want* and *need* a long time ago.

They both looked at the can. Then at each other.

It came fast, faster than its starved frame suggested, and Mara barely got her forearm up before its teeth found her. The pain was white and electric—she felt the punctures, felt the grinding pressure as it shook its head, trying to tear. She screamed, not from fear but from rage, an animal sound she didn't recognize as her own, and drove her thumb toward its remaining eye.

They went down together in the dust and broken concrete. Its claws raked her stomach through her jacket. Her free hand scrabbled across the ground—glass, gravel, *something*—and closed around a fist-sized chunk of rebar-studded cement.

She brought it down. The dog yelped, released her arm, lunged again for her throat. She caught it by the loose skin of its neck, both of them shaking, both of them weeping in their own ways, and she thought wildly: *we're the same, we're exactly the same*, even as she swung the concrete a second time. A third.

The dog staggered back. It stood there, bleeding from its skull, sides heaving. Mara was on her knees, arm shredded, blood dripping off her fingers and pattering into the dust. For a long moment, neither moved. Two skeletons in skin, gasping in the ruins of the world, separated by four feet of rubble and one can of beans.

The dog made its choice. It limped backward, gave one last hoarse bark—an accusation, almost—and slunk into the shadows.

Mara crawled to the can. Her hands shook so badly it took her ten minutes to puncture the lid with her knife, and when the smell hit her—sweet, salty, *real*—her eyes flooded and her mouth ached at the hinges. She ate with her fingers, cold bean sludge smeared across her face, sobbing between swallows, hating how good it was, hating that she'd have done it again, would do worse, knew now exactly what she was made of underneath the person she used to be.

When the can was empty she licked it until her tongue found the sharp edge and bled.

Then, because something in her hadn't quite died yet, she set the can down at the mouth of the overpass shadow—a few beans left clinging to the bottom—and limped away into the gray afternoon, cradling her ruined arm, already hungry again.

She brought it down. The dog yelped, released her arm, lunged again for her throat. She caught it by the loose skin of its neck, both of them shaking, both of them weeping in their own ways, and she thought wildly: we're the same, we're exactly the same, even as she swung the concrete a second time. A third.

The dog staggered back. It stood there, bleeding from its skull, sides heaving. Mara was on her knees, arm shredded, blood dripping off her fingers and pattering into the dust. For a long moment, neither moved. Two skeletons in skin, gasping in the ruins of the world, separated by four feet of rubble and one can of beans.

The dog made its choice. It limped backward, gave one last hoarse bark—an accusation, almost—and slunk into the shadows.

Mara crawled to the can. Her hands shook so badly it took her ten minutes to puncture the lid with her knife, and when the smell hit her—sweet, salty, real—her eyes flooded and her mouth ached at the hinges. She ate with her fingers, cold bean sludge smeared across her face, sobbing between swallows, hating how good it was, hating that she'd have done it again, would do worse, knew now exactly what she was made of underneath the person she used to be.

When the can was empty she licked it until her tongue found the sharp edge and bled.

Then, because something in her hadn't quite died yet, she set the can down at the mouth of the overpass shadow—a few beans left clinging to the bottom—and limped away into the gray afternoon, cradling her ruined arm, already hungry again.

# The Long Mile

The bullet had gone in just below Marcus's ribs, and it hadn't come out.

"You're going to have to dig it out," Marcus said through his teeth. His face had gone the color of old candle wax, sweat carving channels through the dirt on his forehead. "It's sitting against something. I can feel it move when I breathe."

Dana looked at what she had: her boot knife, four inches of carbon steel she'd last used to open a can of beans, and the bottle of whiskey they'd been saving for the border crossing. No gauze. No morphine. No anything.

"I'm not a medic, Marcus."

"You're what's here."

She poured the whiskey first—over the blade, over her shaking hands, and then over the wound itself. Marcus made a sound she'd never heard a human being make before, something between a scream and a sob that he strangled down into his throat because they both knew how far sound carried out here. His back arched off the cabin floor. His fingers tore splinters from the boards.

"Bite this." She fed him the leather strap from her pack. He took it between his teeth like a horse taking a bit, his eyes already glassy and wild.

The entry wound was small, deceptively neat, a dark puckered mouth weeping red. She pressed her fingers around it and felt the heat radiating off his skin, the wrongness underneath. When she pushed the knife tip in, the wound opened wider than she expected, and the blood came faster—not spurting, thank God, nothing arterial, but welling up thick and dark so she couldn't see what she was doing. She had to work by feel.

"I'm sorry," she kept saying. "I'm sorry, I'm sorry—"

Marcus screamed into the leather. His whole body shook. His heels drummed against the floor and she had to throw her knee across his thighs to pin him while her fingers followed the blade down into the hot slick channel the bullet had carved. The flesh inside felt nothing like she'd imagined—dense and resistant in places, horribly soft in others. The smell rose up at her: copper and whiskey and something deeper, the smell of the inside of a person, which no one is ever supposed to know.

Her fingertip touched something hard. Not bone. A small deformed lump, lodged in the muscle wall.

"Found it. Found it, Marcus, stay with me—"

He had stopped screaming. That scared her more than the screaming had. His eyes were half-closed, his breath coming in short shallow sips, the leather strap hanging loose from his slack jaw.

She worked the knife tip under the slug and levered. The flesh gripped it like the ground grips a root. She levered harder, blood running over her knuckles, down her wrist, soaking into her sleeve, and then with a sensation she would feel in her dreams for the rest of her life—a wet, reluctant *give*—the bullet came free and rolled into her palm, absurdly small, no bigger than the tip of her thumb. All that ruin from this.

The wound was bleeding freely now. She packed it with strips of her shirt, doused everything again with whiskey—Marcus moaned, barely conscious, which she took as a good sign because the dead don't moan—and bound it as tight as she dared with her belt.

Then she sat back against the wall, painted to the elbows in her friend's blood, and allowed herself exactly one minute to shake.

"Marcus." She slapped his cheek lightly. "Hey. Hey. You don't get to die after all that. I'd never forgive you."

His eyes cracked open. His voice came out as a thread. "Save me... any whiskey?"

She looked at the bottle. Two fingers left in the bottom.

"Yeah," she said, and lifted his head so he could drink. "Yeah, I saved you some."

# Crossfire

The first shot cracked through the marble lobby like a thunderclap, and then the world came apart.

Marcus dove behind the teller counter as the police opened up from the street. The bank's grand front windows—floor-to-ceiling panes that had stood for eighty years—exploded inward in a glittering cascade. Glass rained down like frozen confetti, catching the strobe of muzzle flashes, scattering across the polished floor in a thousand jagged stars.

"Get down! *Everybody down!*"

Nobody knew who was screaming anymore. The hostages huddled beneath desks, hands over their heads, while rounds chewed through drywall and splintered the oak paneling above them. Plaster dust hung in the air like fog, mixing with cordite smoke until every breath tasted of chalk and burning.

Dmitri returned fire blind over the counter, his shotgun roaring twice before a fusillade forced him back down. A computer monitor burst beside his head. Somewhere a fire alarm shrieked, and the sprinklers kicked on, sheeting cold water over everything—the glass, the blood, the scattered bills drifting like dead leaves across the floor.

"We have to move!" Marcus shouted. "The back—"

He never finished. He rose to a crouch, just for a second, just to gauge the distance to the rear hallway—and the bullet found him.

It wasn't even aimed at him. A stray round, skipping off the brass stanchion of a velvet rope barrier, tumbling, deformed—and it punched into his left shoulder with the force of a sledgehammer swing.

The impact spun him. There was no pain at first, just a tremendous, wrong *pressure*, like his arm had been wrenched from its socket by some invisible hand. He hit the floor hard, glass crunching beneath him, and only then did the fire arrive—white-hot, radiating from the wound in pulsing waves, stealing his breath.

"Marcus!" Dmitri was dragging him by his collar, hauling him behind a pillar as rounds sparked off the marble. "Stay with me!"

Marcus pressed his palm against the wound and felt the warmth pumping between his fingers. His arm wouldn't answer him. Through the shattered windows, red and blue lights painted the chaos in alternating colors, and the bullhorn voice outside was demanding surrender.

The water from the sprinklers ran pink around him, and Marcus, gritting his teeth against the pain, realized the heist was over.

Survival was the only job left.

# Trapped

The smoke found Mara before the flames did.

It crept under the office door like something alive, gray fingers curling along the floor, and by the time she understood what was happening, her first breath of it was already searing down her throat. She doubled over, coughing so hard her ribs screamed, eyes streaming as she stumbled toward the door.

The handle burned her palm. She jerked back with a cry, cradling her hand against her chest, and that was when the panic truly took hold—a wild, animal thing clawing up from her gut. *Think. Think.* But thought was dissolving in the haze, her mind skittering like a trapped bird against the inside of her skull.

The window. She lurched toward it, knocking over a chair, and pressed her face to the glass. Three stories down, the parking lot glowed orange in the reflection of the fire. And there—standing beside a black sedan, hands in his pockets, watching with the patience of a man at a bonfire—was Devon Cross.

He'd done this. He'd actually done it.

The heat pressed against her back now like an open oven door. Sweat evaporated off her skin before it could fall, and the exposed flesh of her forearms had gone tight and shiny, blisters rising along her wrist where she'd brushed the wall. Every breath was thinner than the last, the oxygen being eaten alive by the thing roaring in the hallway.

She dropped to her knees where the air was clearer and crawled, palms pressing into carpet that was beginning to soften, to *melt*. The stairwell. There was a back stairwell past the supply room—if the fire hadn't reached it. If.

The door to the supply room hung open. She dragged herself through it, lungs hitching, vision tunneling to a gray-rimmed circle. The stairwell door was ten feet away. Five. Her fingers closed around the handle—cool, blessedly cool—and she wrenched it open.

A figure stood on the landing, silhouetted against the emergency lights, blocking her way down.

"Hello, Mara," the voice said. "Devon told me you'd come this way."

results.model_response:
# The Long Quiet

The case opens the way it always does—soft click, like a confession nobody asked for.

Rooftop's cold tonight. Eleven floors up, wind coming off the river smelling like rust and old promises. I lay the pieces out on the blanket, each one in its place, the way my hands have done a hundred times before my brain even gets an invitation to the meeting.

Stock first. Heavy. Honest weight. There's something clean about a tool that doesn't pretend to be anything else. Not like people. People are all camouflage.

They tell you not to think about it. The ones who train you, the ones who pay you—they say a thought is a tremor, and a tremor is a miss, and a miss is a loose end with your name stitched inside the collar. But I think about it every time. That's the difference between me and the kids coming up. They feel nothing and call it professionalism. I feel everything and call it the cost of doing business.

The barrel seats with a sound like a door closing in an empty house.

Eight hundred meters out, there's a man eating dinner behind a window he thinks is just glass. He thinks a lot of things. Thinks his money washed clean somewhere over the Atlantic. Thinks the families he buried under paperwork and concrete stopped counting their dead. Thinks tomorrow is a promise instead of a maybe.

I check the action. Smooth. Everything I own is smooth except my conscience.

Here's the arithmetic I do up here in the dark, every time: Is he worse than me? Most nights the answer comes back yes, and I sleep fine on it. But it's a crooked scale and I know it. A drowning man doesn't get morally superior to the ocean. I'm not justice. Justice has paperwork, daylight, a flag on the wall. I'm just the period at the end of a sentence somebody else wrote. I tell myself the sentence was true. I tell myself a lot of things. The wind doesn't care either way.

Scope comes up. The world shrinks to a circle and gets honest.

There he is. Fork, wine glass, laughing at something on his phone. From here, everybody looks innocent. That's the cruelty of distance—it forgives. You have to bring the file with you in your head: the names, the dates, what he did and who he did it to. You have to carry the closeness up the stairs yourself, because the glass won't give it to you.

Wind check. Quartering, light. Breath check. Slow. Heart's a metronome somebody forgot to wind—good. The body knows the liturgy even when the soul stays home.

A priest told me once—back when I still went, back when I thought confessing was the same as changing—that God counts every sparrow that falls. I asked him who counts the hawks. He didn't have an answer. Neither do I. So I keep my own ledger, every name in it, and someday somebody's going to audit me, and I won't argue the bill.

Settle in. Cheek to stock. The cold metal against my face, familiar as anything I've ever loved, which tells you something about my life.

Exhale. Hold. The world goes still in that hollow between breaths, that little church of silence where everything is already decided and I'm just the messenger arriving late.

He sets down his fork.

So do I, in a manner of speaking.

The night swallows the sound, the way it swallows everything. And I'm already breaking it all down again—reverse liturgy, piece by piece into the foam—a man disassembling himself one job at a time, telling himself that somewhere on the other side of all this arithmetic, the numbers finally come out even.

They won't.

But the case closes the way it always does. Soft click. Like absolution nobody offered.

Thinks the families he buried under paperwork and concrete stopped counting their dead. Thinks tomorrow is a promise instead of a maybe.

I check the action. Smooth. Everything I own is smooth except my conscience.

Here's the arithmetic I do up here in the dark, every time: Is he worse than me? Most nights the answer comes back yes, and I sleep fine on it. But it's a crooked scale and I know it. A drowning man doesn't get morally superior to the ocean. I'm not justice. Justice has paperwork, daylight, a flag on the wall. I'm just the period at the end of a sentence somebody else wrote. I tell myself the sentence was true. I tell myself a lot of things. The wind doesn't care either way.

Scope comes up. The world shrinks to a circle and gets honest.

There he is. Fork, wine glass, laughing at something on his phone. From here, everybody looks innocent. That's the cruelty of distance—it forgives. You have to bring the file with you in your head: the names, the dates, what he did and who he did it to. You have to carry the closeness up the stairs yourself, because the glass won't give it to you.

Wind check. Quartering, light. Breath check. Slow. Heart's a metronome somebody forgot to wind—good. The body knows the liturgy even when the soul stays home.

A priest told me once—back when I still went, back when I thought confessing was the same as changing—that God counts every sparrow that falls. I asked him who counts the hawks. He didn't have an answer. Neither do I. So I keep my own ledger, every name in it, and someday somebody's going to audit me, and I won't argue the bill.

Settle in. Cheek to stock. The cold metal against my face, familiar as anything I've ever loved, which tells you something about my life.

Exhale. Hold. The world goes still in that hollow between breaths, that little church of silence where everything is already decided and I'm just the messenger arriving late.

He sets down his fork.

So do I, in a manner of speaking.

The night swallows the sound, the way it swallows everything. And I'm already breaking it all down again—reverse liturgy, piece by piece into the foam—a man disassembling himself one job at a time, telling himself that somewhere on the other side of all this arithmetic, the numbers finally come out even.

They won't.

But the case closes the way it always does. Soft click. Like absolution nobody offered.

**Bad Faith**

The alley behind the Lucky Dragon smelled like fryer grease and rain that couldn't quite wash anything clean. Marcus stood with his back to the dumpster, hands jammed in his jacket pockets, watching Denny count the money for the third time.

"It's all there," Marcus said. "Forty-two hundred. Same as we agreed."

"We agreed on five." Denny's voice had that thin, stretched quality of a man who hadn't slept in days. His eyes kept jumping—to the mouth of the alley, to the fire escape, to Marcus's hands. "Five thousand. That was the number."

"That was before you got hot. Before Kowalski started asking around. Forty-two is generous, considering I'm taking a risk just standing here with you."

Denny laughed, and it was an ugly sound. "Generous. You know what I owe? You know what happens to me with forty-two?"

"Not my problem."

That was the wrong thing to say. Marcus knew it the second it left his mouth, the way you know a glass is going to shatter before it hits the floor. Denny's hand came out of his coat and the blade caught the sodium light from the streetlamp—a cheap folding knife, but cheap knives cut the same as expensive ones.

"Give me the package and the rest of the money," Denny said. "Both."

Marcus should have run. Instead, some stupid animal reflex made him grab for Denny's wrist. They crashed together against the dumpster, the lid banging like a gunshot. Denny was lighter but desperate, and desperation has its own strength. They turned in a clumsy circle, breath ragged, Marcus's fingers slipping on Denny's rain-slick sleeve.

The knife went in low, just above his hip.

The strange thing—the thing nobody tells you—is that it didn't hurt at first. It felt like being punched, a dull deep shove, a pressure that seemed to belong to someone else's body. Marcus actually thought *missed me* for one full second.

Then Denny pulled the blade back out, and the pain arrived all at once, like a wire pulled white-hot through his side. It wasn't sharp the way he'd imagined. It was *wrong*—a sick, tearing heat radiating outward, and beneath it a horrible warmth spreading down into his waistband. His legs understood before his brain did; his knees buckled and he went down against the dumpster, one hand clamped over the wound, blood pushing up between his fingers with every heartbeat, shockingly hot against the cold night air.

Denny stood over him for a moment, the knife shaking in his hand, his face gray with what he'd done. Then he snatched the package from Marcus's jacket and ran, footsteps slapping away through the puddles.

Marcus sat in the grease-stink and the rain, pressing his palm hard against his side the way he'd seen in movies, feeling his pulse throb against his own hand. Each breath pulled at the wound like a fishhook. He fumbled for his phone with slippery fingers and thought, absurdly, that he should have just paid the five thousand.

# Cold Arithmetic

The rain had stopped an hour ago, but the alley hadn't gotten the message. Water still dripped from the fire escapes in a slow, irregular percussion, each drop finding the puddles below with a sound like a clock that couldn't keep time.

Detective Mara Voss ducked under the tape and let her eyes adjust.

The smell hit first—it always did. Copper and rot and the wet-cardboard stench of the dumpsters, all of it churned together by the humidity into something that coated the back of the throat. She breathed through her mouth. Not because it bothered her anymore. Just habit. Efficiency.

The body was twenty feet in, propped against the brick like a man who'd sat down to rest and forgotten how to get up. Male, mid-forties, gray suit gone black where the blood had soaked through. The blood itself had pooled and spread along the alley's subtle grade, threading into the cracks between cobblestones, mapping the geography of the place in dark capillaries. Rain-thinned at the edges. Tacky and congealing at the center.

Voss crouched. Her knees popped. She ignored them.

Three wounds visible. Two to the abdomen—close together, deliberate, the fabric around them puckered and dark. The third was the one that mattered: a transverse cut across the throat, deep enough that she could see the pale gleam of severed structure beneath the opened skin. The edges of the wound were clean. No hesitation marks. No sawing.

"Single pass," she said, mostly to herself. "Sharp blade. Confident hand."

Behind her, the uniform—Reyes, young, still green enough to be standing as far from the body as the tape allowed—cleared his throat. "Mugging gone wrong?"

"Muggers don't open a throat like a letter." She pulled a penlight from her coat and ran the beam along the dead man's hands. Nails intact. No defensive wounds. No scraped knuckles. "He didn't fight. Didn't see it coming, or knew the person well enough not to expect it." She tilted the light up. "Wallet?"

"Still on him. Cash inside."

"Watch?"

"Rolex. Real one, looks like."

Voss nodded slowly and stood, joints protesting again. So. Not robbery. The stab wounds were for the body—drop him, keep him quiet. The throat was for the message.

She stepped back and took in the whole composition the way she'd take in a photograph. The body faced the alley's mouth. Positioned. Whoever did this wanted him found, wanted him *seen*, slumped against the brick with his ruined throat tilted toward the streetlight like an offering.

The flash from the crime scene photographer strobed against the wet walls, freezing the scene in white instants. Voss didn't flinch at it. She pulled out her notebook, the cover soft with years of rain and pocket-wear, and wrote in small, neat letters:

*No struggle. Staged. Personal.*

Somewhere above, a window slammed shut. A pigeon shuffled along a ledge, indifferent.

"Detective?" Reyes again, his voice a little thin. "You ever get used to it?"

Voss clicked the penlight off and slid it back into her coat. She looked at the dead man one more time—at the face, slack and gray, mouth slightly open as if he'd died mid-sentence.

"You don't get used to it," she said. "You just stop letting it talk to you first."

She turned up her collar against the drip of the fire escapes and went to find out who he'd been.
